VA.title: Comparative Report of Local Government Revenues and Expenditures, fiscal 2025
VA.what: Every Virginia county and city reports its spending to the state in these same categories, so the numbers line up from place to place.
VA.scope: day-to-day operations, including the school division
VA.note: This is money spent on day-to-day operations from the general government funds. Education includes the whole school division’s operating spending, paid for with state and federal money as well as local taxes. Capital projects, debt payments and utilities run as businesses are counted separately (below).

NC.agency: North Carolina Department of State Treasurer
NC.title: Annual Financial Information Report (AFIR), county data, fiscal 2025
NC.what: Every North Carolina county files this report with the State Treasurer each year, in the same categories, so the numbers line up from county to county.
NC.spentOn: everything, from all funds (not counting depreciation or money moved between funds)
NC.note: Education is what the county paid to the public schools and the community college, not the schools’ whole budget (the state pays most of that). Debt payments are counted in the total.

GA.title: Report of Local Government Finances, fiscal 2024
GA.fy_label: the fiscal year that ended in 2024
GA.what: Every Georgia county files this report with the Department of Community Affairs each year, using the state’s standard list of government functions, so the numbers line up from county to county.
GA.scope: operations and capital, including utility systems, not debt
GA.spentOn: day-to-day costs and building projects, including utility systems like water and sewer (not counting debt payments or money moved between funds)
GA.note: These are the numbers as the county filed them; they are not audited. Each county picks its own fiscal year, most often ending June 30 or December 31. Consolidated city-county governments (like Athens-Clarke and Augusta-Richmond) also pay for city services. Each “source” link opens the county’s own filed workbook.

MN.agency: Minnesota Office of the State Auditor
MN.title: 2024 Minnesota County Finances Report, raw data
MN.what: Every Minnesota county reports its spending to the State Auditor each year in the same categories, so the numbers line up from county to county.
MN.spentOn: day-to-day costs, building projects and debt payments from its governmental funds (utilities run as businesses are not included)
MN.note: Lines marked “buildings and equipment” are capital spending; the rest are day-to-day costs. The State Auditor does not break “all other general government” down further.

IA.title: County Budgeted Expenditures by Service Area, fiscal 2027
IA.what: Every Iowa county files its budget with the Department of Management using the same ten service areas, so the numbers line up from county to county. The state does not publish finer lines.
IA.spentOn: all funds (not counting money moved between funds)
IA.note: Public safety and legal services combines the sheriff, jail, county attorney and courts. Physical health and social services combines public health, general assistance and veterans services. County environment and education covers conservation, extension and libraries.

IN.agency: Indiana Gateway for Government Units (Department of Local Government Finance)
IN.title: Budget Form 4B, adopted budget estimates, 2026
IN.what: Every Indiana county files its budget through the state’s Gateway site, fund by fund. The state lists funds only; County Commons grouped them into areas by each fund’s name.
IN.scope: all county funds, as adopted (before state review)
IN.spentOn: all its funds, as adopted by the county council (the state may certify less)
IN.note: These are the amounts the county council adopted; the Department of Local Government Finance reviews them and may certify less. Funds include grants and money set aside for one purpose, like federal relief. The “source” link opens the county’s Form 4B in Gateway; pick the year to see it.

KY.title: fiscal court audit, fiscal 2025
KY.fy_label: the fiscal year that ended June 30, 2025
KY.heading: Its budget, from the state audit
KY.what: Kentucky doesn’t publish county budgets in one public place, so these come from each county’s latest audit by the State Auditor, which prints the final budget fund by fund. Audits run a year or more behind.
KY.spentOn: all its funds (not counting money moved between funds)
KY.note: These are the final budget amounts after the fiscal court’s amendments, from the audit’s budget comparison pages. “Administration” is mostly employee benefits and insurance. Each page number opens that page of the audit.

KS.title: certified county budget, 2026
KS.what: Every Kansas county files its certified budget with the state Department of Administration. Its first page lists the most the county may spend from each fund this year. The state lists funds only; County Commons grouped them into areas by each fund’s name.
KS.spentOn: all its funds (the most it is allowed to spend)
KS.note: These are the budget authority amounts from the certificate page: the most the county may spend from each fund. Money moved between funds can be counted in both. Each page number opens that page of the county’s filed budget.

NE.title: county budget filing, fiscal 2025–26
NE.what: Every Nebraska county files its adopted budget with the State Auditor on the same form, so the numbers line up from county to county.
NE.spentOn: all its funds, including money moved between funds
NE.note: These come from the budget form’s Schedule of Budgeted Disbursements. Transfers between funds are included, so some money is counted twice. The cash reserve carried into next year is not counted. Each page number opens that page of the county’s filed budget.
